lines.text: What if the most famous rich men alive lost everything overnight?
lines.tone: slow and curious, a question to the viewer

lines.text: No money. No names. No bank that takes their call.
lines.tone: each short sentence lands, then lighter and quick on the last line

lines.text: Monday, nine in the morning. A courthouse hallway in New York, and one long wooden bench.
Ten men sit on it, shoulder to shoulder, and none of them looks at the others.
Donald Trump fixes his tie in the black screen of his phone. Robert Kiyosaki is telling the guard that debt is a gift.
On Friday they owned towers, rockets, studios and stores. By lunch, a clerk will turn all of it into paperwork.
But nobody will lend them a dollar after today. Not a bank, not a friend, not the man beside them.
They walk out with one thing: whatever is inside their heads.
Well, you'd think that's enough to start again. Five years will show if it was ever skill.
And the best deal of those five years is about to be made on this bench, for forty dollars.
At the far end, Kevin O'Leary reads the others one by one, the way a man reads price tags.
Then he slides along the bench to Elon Musk.

O'Leary leans in, quiet as a banker at a funeral. "Nobody pays for parts before the thing exists, Elon. I will." He holds up two twenties. "Forty dollars. Ten percent of everything you ever build." A pause. "Forever."
lines.tone: low and sly, a held pause, then cold and slow on 'Forever'

lines.text: Down the bench, Trump snorts. "Forty bucks? I tip more than that." O'Leary hands him an envelope too. And Musk, with no other offer in the building, goes very quiet.
lines.tone: a loud scoff on Trump's line, then hushed for Musk

lines.text: Musk signs. O'Leary moves one seat along and holds out the next envelope to Jordan Belfort.
Belfort taps the paper. "Forever's a long word in a contract, Kevin." O'Leary doesn't blink. "It's a short one in a bankruptcy."
lines.tone: Belfort light and cocky, O'Leary flat and dry

lines.text: Belfort reads it to the last line, folds it, and hands it back. O'Leary stands, a thick stack of white envelopes under his arm.
By noon the ten are back on the street, and the city teaches them its first lesson.
Grant Cardone asks a bank for a small loan. The banker types his name, reads the screen, and slides the form back.
Robert Kiyosaki asks for a credit card. Same screen. Same slide.
Donald Trump taps his card at a coffee cart, and the machine beeps twice.
Three cards, three answers. Would any screen say yes to you?
Right. A loan was only ever a stranger's trust with interest on top. And nobody trusts them for a cent.
So the only money they can touch is money they make today, with their hands or with their mouths.
Musk has forty dollars and a parts list. Jordan Belfort has a phone with no numbers in it.
A week later, a supermarket parking lot. Musk has built one good scooter out of three broken ones.
For six hours he has explained its battery to everyone who walks by. Nobody stops.
Belfort watches from the curb with a hot dog. Then he takes the handlebars without asking.
He never mentions the battery. He lets a delivery rider take one free lap of the lot, then names three times Musk's price.
The rider pays cash.

Musk was selling a battery. Belfort sold the man an hour of his evening, and let him taste it first. "People hate owing you," he says. "Now. I want half." They settle on forty-five each, and Musk adds one rule. "Never promise what I haven't built." Belfort looks deeply offended. Then he agrees.
lines.tone: Belfort smooth and pleased, Musk firm and plain, a beat before 'Then he agrees'

lines.text: They shake hands. Neither of them lets go first.
Across the river, a motel by the highway rents rooms by the week. Two men split the cheapest one.

Kiyosaki sits on the bed like it's a stage. "Debt is how the rich get richer." Trump perks up. "Great. Lend me some." Kiyosaki has none. He insists, "The banks will forget." Trump laughs. "My companies went to bankruptcy court six times. The banks never came back first. The cameras did."

lines.text: Trump props his phone on a plastic chair by the empty pool and goes live.
Eleven strangers watch him eat a vending machine sandwich with a knife and fork, like a state dinner.
By midnight, eleven is four thousand. Kiyosaki calls the bank again and gets the voicemail.
So. Week one. Here's the score.

Musk builds, Belfort sells, and they split it down the middle. Trump found an audience. Kiyosaki found a voicemail. O'Leary keeps his envelopes, and waits. And Cardone is still waiting for a bank to say yes.
lines.tone: brisk and wry, a beat after each name

lines.text: Next: six months in, and the first real money.
Six months later, the garage behind the motel smells of solder.
Musk sleeps on a folding cot beside the workbench and rebuilds thirty scooters a month. Every one leaves with Belfort.
Belfort never says lithium. If you deliver food for a living, he sells you one more delivery an hour.
Five more names. Ask yourself which one gets paid first.
Across town, Alex Hormozi walks into dying gyms and offers to fill them. He gets paid only from new members, cash first.
Mark Zuckerberg sits in a public library writing code that finds broken shop websites. Then he fixes them for a fee.
Mark Cuban rents one bicycle to a kid who delivers lunch. Then two bicycles. Then twenty.
Jeff Bezos sells used books off a folding table and writes down every title that sells twice.
But Grant Cardone, making a hundred calls a day, gets a hundred hang-ups.
His deals run on other people's money. His name can't raise it anymore.
By month nine, a hundred thousand people tune in every night to watch Trump eat cereal from a crystal glass.
Uh-oh. One night, Kiyosaki steps into the frame.

He wants to teach them something useful. Trump says, "Two minutes," and hands him the phone. Kiyosaki smiles into the lens. "Lesson one. Your house is not an asset." The count starts falling. Nine hundred gone. Two thousand. Kiyosaki keeps teaching. And Trump's smile gets very, very thin.

Month nine. The score.

The scooters sell. Hormozi's gyms fill. Bezos writes down every book that sells twice. Trump owns the night, alone, and Kiyosaki is out of the picture. And Cardone? A hundred calls a day. A hundred hang-ups.

Year one. Mark Cuban runs two hundred delivery riders out of a warehouse office with no chairs.
He has heard about the scooters that never break down.

Cuban leans on the desk. "How many by Christmas?" Musk answers first. "Fifty. Fifty good ones." Before he can finish, Belfort holds up five fingers. "Five hundred." Cuban doesn't blink. "Five hundred by December twentieth, or you never come back." And Musk hears himself say yes.

In the parking lot, Musk doesn't start the van.

Musk grips the wheel. "You promised what we haven't built." Belfort says, "You said yes." Musk says, "Only because you already had." Belfort shrugs. "Promise, then build. That's how big orders work." Musk looks at him. "That's how fires work."

lines.text: Belfort laughs. Then he sees Musk isn't laughing, and stops.
For eleven weeks the garage lights never go off.
The good cells won't arrive before Christmas, so Musk orders cheap ones from a seller he has never met.
A heat test takes a day per batch. He skips it on the last two hundred.
On the nineteenth of December, five hundred scooters roll into Cuban's warehouse. One day early.
Cuban pays. Belfort frames the receipt.
Three hundred cheap cells are left over on a garage shelf.

A network wants Trump for a show called How to Lose a Billion. Kiyosaki asks, "And what will you own?" Trump spreads his hands. "The audience. The audience paid for this car." Trump pats the roof. "There's a seat in the back for a man who lost everything." Kiyosaki shakes his head. "I teach the lesson. I'm not one." Trump shrugs.

Vance smiles. "And they'll be fine." A beat. "Probably."
